title: In re Williams, Eugene, BIIA Dec., 95 3780 (1998)
text:
Williams, Eugene
BURDEN OF PROOF
Hearing loss
When the evidence shows that a worker continued to be placed in a noisy work
environment after the date of a given audiogram, the burden shifts to the employer to
show by persuasive evidence that the subsequent workplace noise was not injurious to the
workers hearing. ….In re Eugene Williams, BIIA Dec., 95 3780 (1998) [dissent]
[Editor's Note: The burden-shifting requirement set forth by the Board in Williams was reversed
by the Washington State Supreme Court in Boeing v. Heidy 147 Wn.2d 78 (2002).]
OCCUPATIONAL DISEASE (RCW 51.08.140)
Hearing loss
Present methods of differentiating between age-related hearing loss (presbycusis) and
noise-related hearing loss are not sufficiently reliable to allow an award for permanent
hearing loss to be reduced for presence of presbycusis. ….In re Eugene Williams, BIIA
Dec., 95 3780 (1998) [dissent] [Editor's Note: The Board's decision finding that the present
methods of differentiation between aged-related hearing loss (presbycusis) and noise-related
hearing loss as not being sufficiently reliable to allow for permanent hearing loss to be reduced for
presence of presbycusis was affirmed by the Washington State Supreme Court in Boeing v. Heidy
147 Wn.2d 78 (2002). See also, In re Larry Wass, BIIA Dec., 01 11201(2002).]
Schedule of benefits applicable
For claims filed after 1988, the schedule of benefits for an occupational disease is
established as of the date the disease requires medical treatment or becomes totally or
partially disabling. An individual's hearing loss is deemed to require medical treatment
as of the date a person consults with a physician or seeks other means of obtaining relief
from his or her hearing loss. An individual's hearing loss is partially disabling when the
average loss demonstrated by medically valid audiometric testing exceeds 25dB at the
four frequencies specified in the AMA Guides and evidence demonstrates that the worker
knew of the hearing limitations. ….In re Eugene Williams, BIIA Dec., 95 3780 (1998)
[dissent] [Editor's Note: The applicable statute is RCW 51.32.180(b). The Board's decision
requiring that the worker know of the hearing limitations was overruled in Boeing v. Heidy, 147
Wn 2d 78(2002), In re Larry Wass, BIIA Dec., 01 11201 (2002).]

1 ISSUES
2
3 1. Are the present methods of differentiating between age-related hearing
4 loss and industrially-related hearing loss sufficiently reliable that a
5 disability award may be reduced so as to allocate for the suspected
6 presence of age-related hearing loss?
7
8 Answer: No.
9
10 2. Is the Department correct in refusing to consider audiograms dated
11 more than 12 months prior to a worker's last exposure to injurious
12 noise?
13
14 Answer: No. The choice of a 12-month period is not
15 supported by medical, scientific or administrative evidence.
16
17 3. With respect to occupational disease hearing loss claims filed after
18 July 1, 1988, what date should be used to determine the applicable
19 schedule of benefits?
20
21 Answer: The date that, when coupled with knowledge on
22 the worker's part, the disease requires medical treatment
23 or becomes partially disabling, whichever occurs first.
24
25 DECISION
26
27 We begin by noting that the summary of evidence presented by our industrial appeals judge
28
29 in the Proposed Decision and Order dated June 30, 1997, is both accurate and complete. As such,
30
31 the evidence will not be restated here other than for purposes of explanation or emphasis.
32
33 However, by way of providing foundation for our later discussion, it is useful to review certain
34
35 uncontested matters beginning with that portion of the ear that is damaged by exposure to
36
37 excessive noise, the inner ear.
38
39 The record reflects that the internal ear is a remarkably sensitive structure that includes,
40
41 among other things, the semicircular canal, the vestibular nerve, the cochlea and the Organ of
42
43 Corti. The Organ of Corti, found in both the left and right ears, contains some sixteen thousand
44
45 sensory hair cells, each of which is connected to a particular sensory nerve. When stimulated by
46
47
3

1 sound, the hair cell/sensory nerve emits an appropriate nerve signal that is sent in combination with
2
3 other nerve signals to the brain for interpretation and analysis.
4
5 The hair cells are of particular interest in connection with industrially related hearing loss.
6
7 Specifically, the medical community has long recognized that prolonged, excessive noise creates
8
9 an environment in the ear in which the hair cells cannot sustain life, whether the reason be
10
11 mechanical displacement or a simple reduction in blood supply. Several theories have been
12
13 proffered. Whatever the reason, the hair cells actually deteriorate, the hairs wither and the cells
14
15 die. Once a cell is dead, the area once occupied by the cell is replaced by scar tissue that is
16
17 unable to sense sound or transmit nerve signals to the brain. Furthermore, the condition is
18
19 irreversible. Once hair cells are lost, they do not regenerate.
20
21 Post-mortem, it is possible to study the internal ear and determine that hair cell population
22
23 has diminished, the loss being quite evident on microscopic examination. It is not possible,
24
25 however, to always know the precise cause of the loss. In the same fashion that prolonged
26
27 exposure to excessive noise causes hair cells to die, so does the process of aging. Unfortunately
28
29 for our purposes here, physicians are not able to determine which hair cells die from exposure to
30
31 noise and which die from aging. The same part of the ear is affected in each case and the resulting
32
33 scar tissue appears the same whether the cause was noise or age. To compound the uncertainty,
34
35 individuals do not lose hair cells at the same rate as they age. In a situation that is perhaps
36
37 analogous to male baldness, some individuals seem to lose sensory hair cells in their inner ear at a
38
39 comparatively young age while other individuals grow quite old with little apparent loss. Everyone
40
41 seems to respond a bit differently.
42
43 It is also important to recognize that hair cell population may be affected by a host of factors
44
45 other than noise or age. The medical community generally recognizes that loss may occur as a
46
47 result of disease, infection, fever, medications, drug toxicity, stroke, cardiovascular efficiency, body
4

1 chemistry and fatigue. Significantly, it is not fully understood how any two of these factors interact
2
3 in a given individual at a given age. In sum, determining the cause of hair cell loss in the presence
4
5 of multiple potential causes is an extremely difficult task.
6
7 At all times relevant to these appeals, the Department of Labor and Industries has rated
8
9 hearing loss by using the nationally recognized impairment guide as found in the American Medical
10
11 Association's publication, Guides to the Evaluation of Permanent Impairment, 4th ed., (AMA
12
13 Guides). The Guides have been adopted pursuant to the provisions of RCW 51.32.080(2) and
14
15 WAC 296-20-01002 . Although there are other guides that could conceivably be used, the AMA
16
17 Guides have generally been adopted on a nationwide basis to determine hearing impairment.
18
19 There are several peculiarities to the AMA Guides that need to be recognized. First, even
20
21 though the human ear is capable of perceiving sound in the range from 20 hertz (Hz) to 20,000 Hz
22
23 (cycles per second), the AMA Guides only consider hearing loss at four of the frequencies basic to
24
25 speech intelligibility, 500, 1000, 2000 and 3000 Hz. Hearing loss in frequencies above and below
26
27 those discreet levels is not considered, at least for purposes of determining the percentage of
28
29 impairment under the AMA Guides. Second, the AMA Guides do not recognize the presence of
30
31 any compensable disability until an individual has experienced an average of more than 25 decibels
32
33 (dB) hearing loss across the four frequencies measured. This 25 dB threshold, sometimes referred
34
35 to as the "low fence" or the "25 dB fence," is premised on research conducted more than 40 years
36
37 ago wherein individuals with hearing loss of 25 dB or less described their hearing as good whereas
38
39 individuals having hearing loss greater than 25 dB described their hearing as fair or poor. Following
40
41 a period of review, criticism, and analysis, this somewhat subjective threshold has come to be
42
43 recognized as the dividing line between normal and abnormal hearing and has been incorporated
44
45 into the AMA Guides. As an aside, other industrialized countries have different thresholds.
46
47
5

1 The loudness or intensity of sound is measured in decibels. Derived from the average of
2
3 18-24 year old males who have no audiological disease, one decibel is generally regarded as the
4
5 least intensity of sound at which any given tone can be perceived. It should be recognized that
6
7 increasingly intense sound, as measured in decibels, does not proceed on a simple arithmetic
8
9 basis. Although a 10 decibel sound is 10 times more intense than a 1 decibel sound (1 power of
10
11 10), a 20 decibel sound is 2 powers of 10 greater, or 100 times more intense. A 30 decibel sound
12
13 is 1000 times more intense.
14
15 An audiogram is a hearing test administered under controlled circumstances and under an
16
17 established protocol. It forms the foundation of any estimate of hearing loss. As might be
18
19 expected, the failure to follow test protocol can lead to wildly varying results. During an audiogram,
20
21 a test subject is asked to listen for low intensity tones that are gradually increased and decreased in
22
23 volume until the individual's hearing threshold is established for a given frequency. The faintest
24
25 intensity at which an individual is able to perceive a given tone is called the hearing threshold. By
26
27 way of example, a person with a hearing threshold of 25 dB at 500 Hz should not be able to
28
29 perceive a 24 dB sound produced at the same frequency.
30
31 Presbycusis
32
33 Issue No. 1: Are the present methods of differentiating between
34 age-related hearing loss and industrially-related hearing loss sufficiently
35 reliable that a disability award may be reduced so as to allocate for the
36 suspected presence of age-related hearing loss?
37
38 Without question, the bulk of the evidence presented by this appeal relates to the issue of
39
40 presbycusis or age-related hearing loss. The self-insured employer has framed the issue in
41
42 straightforward terms by arguing that an employer should be responsible for only that portion of
43
44 hearing loss that is industrially-related and nothing more. It insists that it should not be required to
45
46 compensate a worker for hearing loss that is essentially the result of aging. The employer correctly
47
points out that the AMA Guides formula for rating hearing impairment does not allocate for
6

1 presbycusis. Neither do the AMA Guides assign causation among two or more possible causes.
2
3 Given these perceived limitations, the employer urges that changes be made to the manner in
4
5 which the Department determines hearing compensability such that a portion of an older worker's
6
7 hearing loss may be recognized to be the result of aging.
8
9 The principal evidence supporting the employer's position is found in the testimony given by
10
11 Robert A. Dobie, M.D., Daniel L. Johnson, Ph.D., and William Ritchie, M.D. Of these three
12
13 witnesses, Dr. Dobie provides a substantial portion of the foundation for the self-insured employer's
14
15 case by virtue of being both the author of Medical-Legal Evaluation of Hearing Loss and the
16
17 architect of a median-based allocation method. Median-based allocation uses epidemiological data
18
19 to predict the most likely cause of a person's hearing loss. Specifically, Dr. Dobie employs
20
21 information taken from several hearing loss studies, including the International Organization of
22
23 Standardization (ISO) 1999 databases,1 A and B, to predict the estimated hearing loss from various
24
25 causes, including age, occupational noise exposure and non-occupational noise exposure.
26
27 Database A contains statistical information from individuals who were grouped according to age
28
29 and then screened to exclude hearing loss from disease, noise exposure and/or injury. Database B
30
31 incorporates survey information that did not involve any screening for hearing loss. By definition,
32
33 Dr. Dobie's method is founded on the use of database medians.
34
35 Dr. Dobie applies the data in the following fashion: estimated hearing loss caused by age is
36
37 divided by the sum of the estimated hearing loss caused by occupational noise plus the estimated
38
39 hearing loss caused by aging. The formula is used to compare an individual's hearing loss with the
40
41 predicted hearing loss of workers of the same age at a comparable level of noise exposure. It
42
43 should be noted that Dr. Dobie considers his method to be primarily useful in situations in which
44
45
46 1 Persons regularly exposed to noise can develop hearing loss of varying severity. Due to this hearing loss, their
47 understanding of speech, perception of everyday acoustic signals, or appreciation of music may be impaired. This
International Standard (ISO 1999) presents in statistical terms the relationship between noise exposures and the noise-
induced permanent threshold shift in people of various ages.
7

1 there is a fundamental lack of objective information in the form of serial audiograms that might
2
3 otherwise assist a physician in determining the cause of hearing loss.
4
5 Dr. Daniel L. Johnson supports Dr. Dobie. He believes that a median-based allocation
6
7 method is an appropriate way of apportioning cause so as to make an equitable determination of
8
9 compensation benefits. Dr. Johnson, who served on the committee that eventually created ISO
10
11 1999, stated that workers are presently being compensated for the entire amount of hearing loss
12
13 whether the loss is industrially-related or not. At the same time, he admitted the primary purpose of
14
15 ISO 1999 is to predict the amount of hearing loss in entire populations that are exposed to certain
16
17 levels of noise. Acknowledging that calculations using ISO databases must be couched in terms of
18
19 statistical models, he conceded that for a single individual it was not possible to precisely determine
20
21 what loss was caused by noise and what was caused by other factors.
22
23 Several witnesses testified in opposition to Dr. Dobie's median-based allocation method.
24
25 They included Aram Glorig, M.D., Henning von Geirke, Ph.D., Francis Irving Catlin, M.D., David M.
26
27 Lipscomb, Ph.D., and Nayak Polissar, Ph.D. Dr. Glorig, who assisted in drafting the hearing loss
28
29 formula promulgated by the American Medical Association (AMA), stated there is no scientific fact
30
31 that allows any deduction or allocation for presbycusis since the interrelationship between injurious
32
33 noise and aging cannot be established. Notwithstanding sections of Exhibit 18, published in 1961,
34
35 and Exhibit 19, published in 1981, it is clear Dr. Glorig's ultimate opinion is that it is wrong to
36
37 attempt to allocate between noise exposure and presbycusis inasmuch as medical science does
38
39 not know how to allocate with any degree of accuracy. It remains unknown whether the relationship
40
41 between age-related hearing loss and noise-related hearing loss is additive, interactive or
42
43 synergistic. Dr. Glorig noted that in drafting the original AMA formula, the problem of presbycusis
44
45 was discussed and eventually resolved with the recognition that there was no known way to deduct
46
47
8

1 for presbycusis. Allocation for presbycusis was not possible based on current scientific information
2
3 and knowledge, particularly at the frequencies encompassed by the AMA formula.
4
5 Dr. Francis Catlin, who acted as chairperson for the AMA Guides committee that concerned
6
7 itself with the ear, nose and throat, essentially agreed. He testified that the American Medical
8
9 Association reviewed the subject and decided that no correction for presbycusis was necessary
10
11 given the AMA Guides formula. He observed that the 25 dB fence, which had been incorporated
12
13 into the AMA Guides formula, would not be exceeded for reasons of age-related hearing loss until
14
15 the age of 75 to 82. Thus, in the vast majority of industrial insurance claims, presbycusis would not
16
17 be an issue. As was the case with Dr. Glorig, Dr. Catlin stated his opposition to the practice of
18
19 using ISO 1999 to predict any individual's hearing loss.
20
21 Dr. Henning von Geirke, who chaired the committee that formulated ISO 1999, further
22
23 confirmed Dr. Glorig's opinion. Dr. von Geirke made it abundantly clear that ISO 1999 is based on
24
25 statistical data and should not be used to assess the hearing impairment of individual persons.
26
27 Statistics cannot accurately predict anything for an individual. ISO 1999 Database B is best used to
28
29 estimate the amount of hearing disability in an entire population. By way of adding further
30
31 emphasis, Dr. von Geirke testified to having served on a National Institute for Occupational Safety
32
33 and Health (NIOSH) committee that considered the matter. The NIOSH committee also concluded
34
35 that no correction should be applied to an individual's audiogram because of age.
36
37 David M. Lipscomb, Ph.D., a clinical and research audiologist, testified that Dr. Dobie's
38
39 methods are flawed for at least two reasons. First, Dr. Dobie ignored the caution that ISO 1999
40
41 Database B contains group data. Database B cannot be applied to individuals because a physician
42
43 does not know where to enter the table. Second, Dr. Dobie assumed that various hearing loss
44
45 causative factors are additive in nature. Dr. Lipscomb insists this is incorrect. The injury factors
46
47 impacting hearing are so complex, both physiologically and psychoacoustically, that it is impossible
9

1 to consider the additive nature of more than one cause of hearing impairment. In any given
2
3 individual, noise could be a 10 percent contributor to hearing loss and age 90 percent, or noise
4
5 could be a 90 percent contributor and age 10 percent. We do not know. Given the present state of
6
7 science and medicine, the foundations for apportioning hearing loss between age and noise are not
8
9 satisfactorily resolved.
10
11 Nayak Polissar, Ph.D., criticized Dr. Dobie's median-based allocation method as being
12
13 statistically suspect. Dr. Polissar, a biostatistician who designs medical research studies with an
14
15 eye toward capturing results in a statistically valid fashion, stated that Dr. Dobie inappropriately
16
17 used data and failed to consider all the different sources of variation and uncertainty. Dr. Polissar
18
19 noted uncertainty in Dr. Dobie's use of smoothed data, uncertainty with combining percentiles
20
21 across hearing tones, uncertainty over test-retest variations, and uncertainties over the variation in
22
23 population data. In the final analysis, Dr. Polissar doubted that opinions based upon Dr. Dobie's
24
25 median-based allocation method could be rendered on a more probable than not basis.
26
27 Mary Burbage, an Adjudicator 5 with the self-insurance section of the Department of Labor
28
29 and Industries, testified to being responsible for managing appeals of hearing loss claims within the
30
31 Department. In those instances in which medical evidence demonstrates that a particular
32
33 non-occupational disease causes hearing impairment, the Department will conceivably segregate
34
35 that portion of hearing loss as being outside the employer's responsibility, assuming medical
36
37 evidence is sufficient to support such. Ms. Burbage indicated that the Department does not,
38
39 however, deduct or segregate for age-related hearing loss under the belief that the 25 dB threshold
40
41 incorporated in the AMA Guides formula takes presbycusis into consideration. We pause to
42
43 observe that the Department appears to be mistaken in this regard. Although the 25 dB threshold
44
45 may, as a practical matter, have the effect of taking a deduction for presbycusis, it is clear from the
46
47
10

1 evidence presented here that the 25 dB threshold and presbycusis have no direct connection with
2
3 one another.
4
5 We are persuaded that the Department's refusal to accept medical opinions founded upon
6
7 Dr. Dobie's median-based allocation method is in keeping with the meaning of RCW 51.32.080(2)
8
9 and WAC 296-20-01002. Our reasons are several. First, Dr. Dobie's median-based allocation
10
11 method has not been recognized on a national basis as a reliable way to segregate noise-induced
12
13 and age-related hearing loss. Second, Dr. Dobie's method takes data from ISO 1999 population
14
15 studies and inappropriately applies it to individuals. ISO 1999 states, "[t]his International Standard
16
17 is based on statistical data and therefore shall not be used to predict or assess the hearing
18
19 impairment or hearing handicap of individual persons." ISO 1999-1990 at 1. Third, the
20
21 preponderance of medical evidence supports the conclusion that injury factors impacting hearing
22
23 are so complex that it is impossible to consider the additive nature of more than one cause of
24
25 hearing impairment. Dr. Dobie's reliance on the principle that multiple causes of hearing loss are
26
27 numerically additive is simply not supported by the greater medical community. Given the present
28
29 state of medicine, the preponderance of evidence forces the conclusion that the foundations for
30
31 apportioning between age and noise are not adequately satisfied. Fourth, Dr. Dobie's
32
33 median-based method of allocation appears to be statistically unreliable. We find Dr. Polissar's
34
35 criticisms sufficiently persuasive to conclude that Dr. Dobie's method of apportionment cannot
36
37 support a medical opinion on a more probable than not basis. Fifth, we find nothing in the Industrial
38
39 Insurance Act that either promotes or encourages the theory that a reduction of an individual's
40
41 permanent partial disability award may be based upon age. To the contrary, RCW 51.12.010
42
43 requires the act to be liberally construed for the purpose of reducing to a minimum the suffering and
44
45 economic loss arising from injuries and/or death occurring in the course of employment. In our
46
47 view, the requirement of liberal construction argues against taking a deduction for presbycusis
11

1 given the competing arguments regarding it. Finally, even if it was medically possible to allocate
2
3 between noise-related and age-related hearing loss, it does not appear that presbycusis, in and of
4
5 itself, rises to the level of compensability until the age range of 75 to 82. As noted earlier, the AMA
6
7 Guides incorporate a 25 dB fence into the hearing loss formula below which hearing loss is
8
9 considered non-compensable. The evidence here indicates that age-related hearing loss will not
10
11 reach the 25 dB threshold of compensability until the age of 75 to 82, thus making the issue of age-
12
13 related hearing loss moot in the vast majority of cases. Even this assumption, that age-related
14
15 hearing loss is not a factor until later in life (75 to 82 years of age), is a statistical conclusion that is
16
17 not descriptive of an individual case. Again, we will not extrapolate from the general to the specific.
18
19 Audiograms
20
21 Issue No. 2: Is the Department correct in refusing to consider
22 audiograms dated more than 12 months prior to a worker's last
23 exposure to injurious noise?
24
25 The next question concerns how to determine a worker's permanent hearing impairment.
26
27 Permanent impairment is determined by audiograms, which measure the loss of hearing. In order
28
29 to measure hearing loss it would be ideal to do an audiogram on the day a worker leaves
30
31 employment. However, few workers are given an audiogram on the day they retire, terminate
32
33 employment, or are otherwise removed from exposure to excessive noise. In cases involving older
34
35 workers, it is not uncommon for audiograms to bracket a worker's retirement by periods of a year or
36
37 more on each side of the date on which employment was terminated. But for the fact that the
38
39 results of the audiograms are often substantially different, this would not be a problem. However,
40
41 an audiogram taken a year or two before retirement may show substantially less impairment than
42
43 an audiogram taken a year or two after retirement.
44
45 Our review of the record indicates that for all times relevant to these appeals the Department
46
47 adhered to a internal rule of practice that disfavored audiograms administered more than 12 months
12

1 prior to a worker's last exposure to injurious noise. Mary Burbage, identified in the previous
2
3 section, testified that audiograms administered more than 12 months prior to a worker's last
4
5 exposure to injurious noise are rejected because they fail to account for additional hearing damage
6
7 that occurs between the date of the audiogram and the date the worker is removed from injurious
8
9 noise. The exceptions to this rule are those instances in which the employer can establish no
10
11 injurious noise existed during the period subsequent to the audiogram in question.
12
13 The self-insured employer argues that the Department's unwritten rule is without substance
14
15 and is patently arbitrary. It insists there is no medical, scientific or administrative reason for
16
17 rejecting any particular audiogram and points out that the Department has been unable to identify a
18
19 statute, code section, or precedent that specifically supports the 12-month rule. The employer
20
21 further notes the Department has failed to explain why a 12-month standard is preferable to a
22
23 1-month, 6-month or 18-month standard.
24
25 In this instance, the employer is correct. The Department has been unable to articulate why
26
27 an audiogram administered 11 months prior to removal from injurious noise is acceptable for rating
28
29 permanent impairment while one administered 13 months prior is not. When subjected to this
30
31 scrutiny, the choice of 12 months appears to be a decision that is not easily supported. At best, the
32
33 12-month rule provides the Department with a working rule of thumb that allows for consistency in
34
35 the administration of claims, whether or not the rule is otherwise supportable.
36
37 Given the record here, there appears to be no particular period of time that can be said to be
38
39 superior over any other. The criticisms brought against a 12-month period apply equally to the
40
41 selection of any other specified period of time. As such, we are unable to conclude that the
42
43 Department's choice of a 12-month period is warranted.
44
45 With that said, we must also address the concerns of the worker. In doing so, we are unable
46
47 to conclude that a worker who continues to be exposed to injurious noise through the final day of
13

1 his or her employment is fairly compensated for hearing loss when his or her disability award is
2
3 based on an audiogram administered months or years earlier. In the presence of sufficiently
4
5 intense sound, we can well imagine a worker suffering permanent hearing loss after only a few
6
7 days of continuous exposure. Given that fact, we are not prepared to conclude that the final days
8
9 of a worker's exposure to excessive noise are so insignificant that any resultant hearing loss can be
10
11 disregarded outright. To do so would be to engage in the same type of assumptions that resulted in
12
13 the Department's 12-month rule.
14
15 The employer argues that a physician may base his or her opinion on an audiogram of any
16
17 given date. We do not necessarily disagree. A physician's opinion could conceivably be based on
18
19 an infinite number of chronologically separate and distinct facts. However, in those instances
20

31

33

37
38 requires the selection of a date specific from, often times, numerous possibilities.

45
46 the time the loss is experienced. While this concept has a certain logic, we are unable to find any
47

2
3 proposal that appears to be outside the province of the Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals.

6
7 appeal) relate to claims filed after July 1, 1988. RCW 51.32.180(b), as amended by Laws of 1988,

10

12 occupational diseases shall be established as of the date the disease
13 requires medical treatment or becomes totally or partially disabling,
14 whichever occurs first, and without regard to the date of the contraction
15 of the disease or the date of filing the claim.

18

23 date of the contraction of the disease or the date of filing the claim."

25 In a series of appeals involving claims filed before July 1, 1988, we determined that the date
26
27 of manifestation of an occupational disease is the particular point in time that determines schedule

30
31 Dec., 89 2737 (1989); In re Milton May, BIIA Dec., 87 4016 (1989); In re Otto Weil, Dec'd, BIIA
32
33 Dec., 86 2814 (1987); and, In re Robert Wilcox, BIIA Dec., 69,954 (1986). Given the 1988
34
35 amendment to RCW 51.32.180, an obvious question is raised as to whether the 1988 Legislature
36
37 created a new rule for determining schedule of benefits or whether the Legislature was merely
38
39 clarifying what was meant by the "date of manifestation."
40
41 We considered this question some years ago. At the time, we specifically concluded that the
42
43 1988 Legislature clarified the meaning of date of manifestation by defining it as "the date the
44
45 disease requires medical treatment or becomes totally or partially disabling, whichever occurs
46
47 first . . .." In re Kenneth Alseth, BIIA Dec., 87 2937 (1989). At first blush, it would appear that the
16

1 matter is long since decided and that the 1988 amendments to RCW 51.32.180 confirm the well
2
3 established "date of manifestation" rule. However, because Alseth involved a claim filed before
4
5 July 1, 1988, some of the Alseth language must be regarded as dicta and is not necessarily
6
7 controlling in the matter before us now. Given the concerns raised by the parties in this appeal, we
8
9 pause to consider whether our reasoning in Alseth remains valid. In doing so, we begin by
10
11 analyzing the phrases "the date the disease requires medical treatment" and "partially disabling" as
12
13 found in RCW 51.32.180(b). We consider the phrase "totally disabling" to be beyond the scope of
14
15 our consideration.
16
17 In the context of industrially-related hearing loss, the phrase "the date the disease requires
18
19 medical treatment" has created more controversy than might first be apparent. Both the claimant
20
21 and the Department of Labor and Industries argue that noise-induced hearing loss is a disease for
22
23 which there is no medical treatment, per se. The "treatment" for noise-induced hearing loss is to
24
25 simply remove the individual from the offending noise. The Department and the claimant argue
26
27 there can be no date of first treatment for hearing loss because noise-induced hearing loss does
28
29 not lend itself to medical treatment in the same sense that other occupational diseases do. Rather,
30
31 noise-induced hearing loss is a condition that can only be identified, monitored and ameliorated
32
33 with hearing aids.
34
35 The concerns raised by the Department and the claimant are well taken. However, the
36
37 parties advance a definition of treatment that appears to be unnecessarily narrow. Conceivably,
38
39 there are many occupational diseases that can neither be cured nor ameliorated by known medical
40
41 treatment. Potentially, many will only be identified, monitored and improved with medical care. To
42
43 require the definition of treatment to be limited to those conditions that can be improved by medical
44
45 care is to focus on the result rather than the process. We decline to accept this limited view. We
46
47 conclude that an individual's hearing loss is deemed to "require medical treatment" as of the date a
17

1 person consults with a physician or seeks other means of obtaining relief from his or her hearing
2
3 loss, irrespective of whether or not curative treatment is available in the usual sense.

5 The second phrase of RCW 51.32.180 relates to the words "partially disabling." As we
6

8
9 any hearing disability until an individual's average hearing loss exceeds 25 dB at the four
10
11 frequencies tested. For purposes of establishing a schedule of benefits date, other hearing loss
12
13 thresholds could be adopted that might begin with as little as 1 dB of permanent threshold shift,
14
15 assuming such a threshold was nationally recognized. To adopt a different standard, however,
16

18

20

22

24
25 purpose of establishing the schedule of benefits date. So that we are clear, we conclude that
26

28
29 25 dB across the frequencies specified in the AMA Guides. Individuals whose threshold shift
30
31 averages 25 dB or less do have some hearing loss, however, their hearing loss will not be
32
33 considered "partially disabling" within the meaning of RCW 51.32.180 until it exceeds, on average,
34

36
37 evaluation or until the Guides are modified.

39 This leads to another and yet more difficult question: Is audiometric evidence sufficient, in
40
41 and of itself, to establish the date at which hearing loss becomes disabling? To briefly frame the
42
43 problem, audiometric testing, which forms the foundation of measuring hearing loss, is not a matter
44
45 that has remained within the exclusive domain of the medical profession. To the contrary,
46
47 audiograms are routinely administered by many non-medical retail businesses, including
18

1 department stores, as well as by employers who administer the tests at the work site, as the record
2
3 here indicates. The validity of an audiometric test should be established by medical opinion that
4
5 confirms the reliability of the test in terms of its administration and results. In light of the significant
6

8

10
11 Although there is no authority directly on point to guide us with regard to the need for
12
13 medical validation, we can reason by analogy. We note, for example, that WAC 296-20-200(2)
14
15 requires determinations of total or partial disability be based on medical opinion. Similarly,
16
17 certification of temporary total disability benefits (time loss compensation) is a decision typically
18
19 made by medical experts as is the decision as to whether a worker requires further treatment.
20
21 While we recognize there is a qualitative distinction between rating percentage of disability, for
22
23 example, and deciding whether hearing loss is or is not disabling, we nonetheless see a pattern
24
25 throughout the Industrial Insurance Act that requires input from medical professionals. This pattern
26
27 leads us to believe that medical evidence is desirable in determining when an individual's hearing
28
29 loss has become disabling so as to avoid inadvertent or misinformed decisions. The sensibility of
30
31 this requirement seems obvious to us. Given that, we conclude that the existence of audiometric
32
33 evidence is not sufficient by itself to establish a schedule of benefits date. The results of
34
35 audiometric testing must be confirmed by medical evidence and/or opinion for the results to form
36
37 the foundation for schedule of benefits.
38
39 A valid and reliable audiometric test that shows than an individual's noise-induced hearing
40
41 loss is partially disabling (greater than 25 dB) would, in the absence of further critical inquiry, seem
42
43 to establish the date for the schedule of benefits. However, noise-induced hearing loss is a peculiar
44
45 occupational disease. Occurring over a period of years, there are no dramatic symptoms to alert an
46
47 individual that hearing loss is progressing. Because it does not cause pain and has no physical
19

1 outward signs or symptoms, hearing loss lacks the element of warning common to other medical
2
3 conditions. Therefore, the nature of hearing loss has the potential to affect workers differently with
4
5 regard to the partially disabling requirement of RCW 51.32.180(b). Workers with a more obvious
6

8
9 work environment is having some adverse effect on them. If these more obvious conditions rise to
10

12

14
15 comparison, hearing loss can become partially disabling without the worker being alerted to the
16

18
19 that would treat workers differently based solely on the nature of the medical condition they may
20
21 have.
22
23 In order to ensure that the "partially disabling" trigger to start the schedule of benefits for
24

26
27 the worker knows of limitations in his or her hearing. Initially individuals may not perceive changes
28
29 in their hearing because these changes are gradual. The adaptation to these changes in hearing
30
31 are often intuitive rather than conscious or deliberate. Eventually a person will know of hearing
32
33 limitations because of interactions with other people or because the circumstances of daily living
34

36
37 problem, but a knowledge that the capacity to hear is not what it once was. Until a person reaches
38
39 this point they are not in a similar position with those who have more obvious occupational
40
41 diseases. When a worker has knowledge of the condition he or she can finally make decisions
42
43 regarding treatment and continued exposure.

45 In the early history of workplace audiometric testing, results were not always or consistently
46
47 made available to the worker. Assuming that such a test were valid, as we have defined it here,
20

1 and assuming that the worker was unaware of the results of such a test, it would be patently unfair
2
3 to utilize the date of such a test to trigger the schedule of benefits. What we require is that there be

10

12

17 We restate and expand on our reasons for requiring knowledge as follows: First, the 25 dB
18

20

24
25 his or her hearing shifts from an average of 25 dB to an average of 26 dB. In the absence of
26

30

36

38
39 who is in a position of ignorance. We will not impose a schedule of benefits on an individual who
40
41 may be unaware that he or she has any limitation in hearing. Fourth, the knowledge element is
42

1 DISSENT
2
3 I strongly disagree with the majority's analysis and legal conclusions on the issues of the
4
5 employer's responsibility for permanent partial disability and the appropriate schedule of benefits on
6
7 hearing loss claims. On the issue of determining which audiogram should be used to determine
8
9 permanent partial disability, I agree in part and disagree in part.
10
11
12 EXTENT OF PERMANENT PARTIAL DISABILITY
13
14 The statement of the first issue as presented by the majority is not accurate. The issue is
15
16 simply whether the formula used by the Department to calculate Mr. Williams' permanent partial
17
18 disability award for hearing loss should only consider the effects of occupational noise exposure.
19
20 And if so, on a more probable than not basis, what portion of Mr. Williams' hearing loss as of
21
22 May 15, 1995, was occupationally related?
23
24 In addition, the majority's reference to the "suspected presence" of age-related hearing loss
25
26 in this case indicates a collective indifference to a fundamental, uncontested medical fact that forms
27
28 a cornerstone of the employer's grievance. All of the medical experts agree that a portion of
29
30 Mr. Williams' hearing loss is age-related. We are dealing with the actual presence of age-related
31
32 hearing loss, not a "suspected" presence.
33
34 Under the Industrial Insurance Act, a worker is only entitled to compensation for conditions
35
36 that are proximately caused by employment. RCW 51.32.180; RCW 51.08.140; Dennis v.
37
38 Department of Labor & Indus., 109 Wn.2d 476 (1987). For workers' compensation purposes,
39
40 physicians are routinely requested to provide opinions on the conditions and permanent impairment
41
42 proximately caused by the industrial injury or the occupational disease. In occupational hearing
43
44 loss claims the Department utilizes the American Medical Association's Guides to the Evaluation of
45
46 Permanent Impairment, 4th ed., (AMA Guides) to determine the extent of permanent impairment.
47
While the Department has historically allocated other causes of hearing loss from the permanent
30

1 partial disability award, they do not allocate for presbycusis. The employer brings this appeal in
2
3 response to the Department's refusal to separate out that portion of the award attributable to
4
5 age-related hearing loss.
6
7 The testimony reflects that the Department's policy of awarding permanent partial disability
8
9 for occupational hearing loss was based on a mistaken belief that the 25 decibel (dB) threshold, in
10
11 effect, allocated any age-related hearing loss suffered by the claimant. The testimony also shows
12
13 that the purpose of the AMA Guides is to provide physicians with guidelines for rating total
14
15 impairment from all causes. They do not include specific guidelines to assist physicians in
16
17 determining the cause of impairment or more importantly, methods for determining the proportion
18
19 of impairment when more than one cause is evident. However, the AMA Guides do provide general
20
21 guidelines to physicians for making causation decisions and stress the importance of acquiring,
22
23 reviewing and analyzing records dating from the onset of the condition, including the results of
24
25 occupational or environmental surveys and test results.
26
27 The cause of a disability or specific condition can only be reached after evaluating the
28
29 individual's medical and work history with other pertinent medical information that exists in that
30
31 individual's case. A physician must use a deductive process that is neither an exact science nor a
32
33 mathematical formula. For occupational hearing loss claims, the AMA Guides do not supplant the
34
35 need for the physician to determine the cause of the hearing loss. Medical opinion must relate the
36
37 condition to employment on a more probable than not basis. Stampas v. Department of Labor &
38
39 Indus., 38 Wn.2d 48 (1951).
40
41 Several nationally recognized medical witnesses testified for the Department and the
42
43 employer on the issue of hearing loss and allocation. There was universal agreement that the
44
45 25 dB low fence is not included in the AMA Guides formula as a means of adjusting for age-related
46
47
31

1 hearing loss. Furthermore, the formula does not adjust for age-related hearing loss. Lastly, the
2
3 AMA Guides do not prohibit an allocation or adjustment for age-related hearing loss.
4
5 Upon failing to demonstrate that the AMA formula adjusts for presbycusis either directly or
6
7 indirectly, the Department then seeks to justify its position by saying that it is not scientifically and
8
9 medically possible to differentiate presbycusis from noise-induced hearing loss. The majority,
10
11 seizing upon this claim of medical and scientific impossibility, declares that the "greater medical
12
13 community" is unable to allocate for presbycusis on a more probable than not basis. Rather than
14
15 showing medical and scientific impossibility, this record shows that for many years there has been
16
17 an ongoing debate among physicians specializing in hearing disorders about how to allocate
18
19 age-related hearing loss. This record clearly provides a reasonable methodology for apportionment
20
21 of causes, disputing the notion of impossibility.
22
23 I am concerned with the way the majority has ignored Dr. Robert Dobie's credentials and
24
25 testimony. Dr. Dobie is a world renowned expert in otology, with extensive involvement in national
26
27 hearing loss developments with the AMA and the American Academy of Otolaryngology. His
28
29 credentials are unimpeachable. The majority narrowly focuses on Dr. Dobie's proposed allocation
30
31 method as a "median-based allocation method." The import of his testimony goes beyond that
32
33 acknowledged by the majority. Dr. Dobie's testimony describes the clinical process used by
34
35 otolaryngologists for determining causation of hearing loss. He emphasizes the importance of a
36
37 physician's experience, knowledge and judgment in evaluating all of the available information and
38
39 deciding which information has the most qualitative value and relevancy to the patient. He stresses
40
41 that the evaluation of hearing loss for causation and allocation is, optimally, based on quality noise
42
43 exposure data and a series of audiograms taken over a period of years that allow the physician to
44
45 compare patterns and trends. This comparison allows the physician to evaluate the reliability of the
46
47 test results, the frequencies in which the loss has occurred, and the rate of loss in order to
32

1 determine probable causes. An asymmetrical pattern may indicate causes other than noise or
2
3 aging.
4
5 Dr. Dobie testified that epidemiological data is useful to physicians in making judgments
6
7 about causation in "doubtful" cases where very little information about an individual is available. He
8
9 cautions that his median-based allocation method should be used only by an informed physician.
10
11 He notes the difference between the level of scientific certainty required when conducting research
12
13 and the level of certainty required in making day-to-day clinical decisions. His appreciation for the
14
15 differences in these standards accounts for his ability to set forth a useful method of apportionment
16
17 between noise-induced and age-related hearing loss. He is aware that this method cannot provide
18
19 a precise percentage allocation, but that for compensation purposes on "doubtful individual cases,"
20
21 it can be used to offer an opinion on work related and age-related hearing loss on a more
22
23 probable than not basis.
24
25 I find it baffling that the Board majority insists that hearing loss is so unique from other types
26
27 of permanent partial disability that it is appropriate for the Department to ignore a medically
28
29 accepted method for segregating unrelated causes of hearing loss. This record clearly
30
31 demonstrates that there is a medically acceptable method. Although not a precise mathematical
32
33 method of allocation, it is nonetheless used by treating otolaryngologists in Washington's medical
34
35 community. While some physicians do not agree, others use it and believe it to be reasonably
36
37 accurate on a more probable than not basis.
38
39 The majority concludes that Dr. Glorig's ultimate opinion is that it is wrong to allocate
40
41 because there is no scientific degree of accuracy. In fact, Dr. Glorig specifically recognized that the
42
43 issue of determining presbycusis allocation is a "legal" problem rather than a scientific one. The
44
45 majority fails to appreciate the distinction between the standard of scientific certainty used in
46
47 medical studies and the standard of legal probability. By focusing on the statistical/mathematical
33

1 and scientific criticisms of the Dr. Dobie's specific allocation method, the Board misses the point of
2
3 a median based allocation method completely. The method is not intended to arrive at a calculation
4
5 on apportionment with absolute scientific and statistical accuracy. This has never been the
6
7 standard for medical testimony in workers' compensation cases. The goal is to provide the
8
9 physician with an additional resource that, when used in conjunction with their medical expertise
10
11 and clinical judgment, allows them to provide an opinion that meets the legal standard of proof in
12
13 workers' compensation cases. Neither the Department nor the Board should dictate to physicians
14
15 as to how they arrive at medical judgments or opinions. To do so has the potential of conflicting
16
17 with one of the basic tenets of workers' compensation--sure and certain relief for the worker.
18
19 In claims for conditions other than hearing loss, while the physician may be asked to explain
20
21 the basis for their opinion, their underlying knowledge and medical assumptions are not laid open to
22
23 scientific scrutiny. Other types of workers' compensation cases rely on physicians and their
24
25 expertise. The same standard should be applied in hearing loss cases.

44 by employment. The majority's direction may sound reasonable, but they fail to recognize the

46 countless fact patterns encountered by claims adjudicators in the thousands of hearing loss claims

40 occupational diseases shall be established as of the date the disease
41 requires medical treatment or becomes totally or partially
